title: Tuo Zaafi with Ayoyo
author: Adwoa Fofie
desc: The fully quantified version — one cup of corn flour to two thirds of cassava, ten cups of loosely packed ayoyo, and a marinade with African nutmeg and selim.
longDesc: This is the most completely measured tuo zaafi in print, and it gives all three components. The swallow is a cup of corn flour and two thirds of a cup of cassava flour in four and a half cups of water, stirred the way you would stir amala or banku, simmered ten minutes and then mixed again until smooth. The ayoyo is ten cups of fresh leaves blended semi-smooth with two cups of water, two tablespoons of dawadawa and shrimp powder. The stew carries the other half of a marinade built on anise, cloves, star anise, African nutmeg, selim and bay.
ingredients: 600 g beef or goat chunks — choose cuts with a bit of fat
Pepper, as much as you need
10 cups fresh ayoyo, loosely packed — discard thick stems
2 smoked mackerel, each cut into 3 pieces
steps: Blend the marinade ingredients. Cook the beef with half of it over medium heat, covered, until soft — check every 15 minutes or so.
For the ayoyo: blend the leaves with the 2 cups of water until semi-smooth.
Cook the blended ayoyo with the dawadawa, onion, shrimp powder and dried herring over medium heat 5 minutes.
For the stew: fry the sliced onion until translucent, then add the rest of the marinade.
Cook 3 minutes, then add the tomato paste.
Cook 3 minutes, then add the blended tomatoes and the cooked beef with its stock.
Simmer about 30 minutes, or until thickened to the consistency you want.
For the tuo: combine the corn flour with the water over medium-low heat and add half a teaspoon of salt.
Keep stirring as you would for amala, banku or a choux pastry.
Simmer 10 minutes, then start the mixing process again until smooth and lump-free, working in the cassava flour.
Stir a further 3 minutes, then scoop into a bowl.
Serve the tuo first, then the ayoyo, then the stew.
chefTips: Her stirring comparison is the most useful line here: keep stirring as you would for amala, banku or a choux pastry. If you have made any of those, you know the resistance you are after.
Ten cups of ayoyo loosely packed is a lot of leaf and it collapses to very little. Discard the thick stems first.
Blend the ayoyo semi-smooth, not smooth. Some leaf structure survives and that is what gives the slipperiness its body.
Check the meat every fifteen minutes or so rather than trusting a total time. Goat and beef vary enormously.
Simmer the tuo ten minutes BETWEEN two rounds of mixing. That rest-and-remix is what gets rid of the lumps.
Her marinade is unusually aromatic for a northern dish — anise, cloves, star anise, African nutmeg, selim and rosemary. The rosemary is not traditional; the rest are.
Half the marinade goes into the meat and half into the stew. Keep the split.
commonMistakes: Leaving the thick ayoyo stems in.
All the marinade into the meat.
Skipping the ten-minute simmer between mixings.
sources: Adapted from 'Tuo Zaafi & Ayoyo', adwoafofie.com. BYLINE AS PRINTED: 'Written By Adwoa Fofie'. Date printed 'Jun 13' WITH NO YEAR. Yield as printed: '4 servings'. Her note: 'This dish is from the Northern part of Ghana.' Quantities confirmed across two fetches except where marked.

Ingredients exactly as printed. Main: 1 cup corn flour; 2/3 cup kokonte/cassava flour; '600g beef/goat chunks (choose cuts that have a bit of fat)'. Marinade: 1 large onion; 'pepper, as much as you need'; 2 tablespoons ginger; 2 tablespoons garlic; 1/2 teaspoon anise; 1/4 teaspoon cloves; '1-star anise'; 1/2 teaspoon dried rosemary; 1 African nutmeg; 2 grains of Selim; 1 bay leaf. Ayoyo: '10 cups fresh ayoyo* loosely packed (discard thick stems)'; '2 tablespoons dawadawa (fermented locust beans)*'; 1 small onion roughly chopped; 2 cups water for ayoyo; 2 tablespoons shrimp powder; 5 small pieces of dried herrings (optional) — THE ASTERISK FOOTNOTES WERE NOT CAPTURED. Stew: 1 large onion sliced; 2 smoked mackerel, each cut into 3 pieces; rest of the marinade; 1/2 cup palm oil/veg oil; 1 1/3 cups blended fresh tomatoes; 1/4 cup tomato paste; 1 teaspoon curry powder; 1 tablespoon shrimp powder. Tuo: '1 cup corn flour+ 4 1/2 cups water'; 2/3 cups cassava flour. THE '4 1/2 CUPS WATER' IS SINGLE-PASS and therefore unverified.

Method quoted: beef and half the marinade over medium heat, 'Cover and allow to cook until soft', 'Check on the meat every 15 minutes or so'. 'Blend the ayoyo and water (if you are using okro, this is the time to add it) until semi-smooth.' 'Cook over medium heat for 5 mins.' Stew: 'Fry until onion is translucent then add the rest of the marinade', 'Cook for 3 mins then add the tomato paste', 'cook for 3 mins then add the blended tomatoes and the cooked beef together with the stock', 'allow the stew to simmer for about 30 minutes or until it's thickened into the consistency you want.' Tuo: 'Place over medium-low heat and add 1/2 a teaspoon of salt.' 'Keep stirring like you would if you were making say amala, banku, or a choux pastry.' 'Allow the tuo to simmer for 10 mins then start the process of mixing again until you get a smooth lump-free mixture.' 'Keep stirring for an additional 3 mins then scoop from the pan and place in a bowl.'

THE FLOUR DISAGREEMENT ACROSS SOURCES, unreconciled. Fran Osseo-Asare: MILLET, with fonio in the Tamale original (GHA044). Fofie here: 1 cup corn flour to 2/3 cup cassava flour. Steyn Hoogakker / ICLEI Africa: 400g corn to 150g cassava, while noting millet is the more indigenous choice (GHA074). GAIN 2016 ethnography: 'whole grain maize flour'. Whitby 1968: millet and guinea-corn. FIVE SOURCES, FOUR DIFFERENT GRAIN SYSTEMS. Nothing averaged.

THE AYOYO HANDLING DISAGREEMENT, also unreconciled: 'Blend... until semi-smooth' here; 'Blend it or keep stirring with... ijabe' (Hoogakker); Whitby 1968 says 'The leaves are not mashed but cut into small pieces prior to cooking and cooked for only about 10 minutes'; and a source flagged for its byline says to 'beat the leaves with your ladle until it becomes slimy with bubbles'.

COOKING TIME for the tuo across sources: about 10 plus 10 minutes (Osseo-Asare); 10 plus 3 minutes here; 15-20 minutes (Pulse Ghana); 'about ten minutes or longer if the quantity is large' (Whitby 1968).

THE OLDEST DESCRIPTION, Whitby 1968, verbatim: 'To make tuo zaafi the flour is sprinkled by handfuls on to boiling water and stirred in. It is cooked on fire with vigorous stirring for about ten minutes or longer if the quantity is large and then eaten with soup.' Also, and this matters for naming: 'The word used for this dish in [s]outhern Ghana is tuo zaafi (Hausa)... each of the northern languages has a different name for it.' The OCR is garbled at '[s]outhern'.
THE NAME, two readings recorded: The Ghana Cookbook headnote gives "'tee zed,' said to mean 'very hot' in Hausa and Dagbani"; a rejected unbylined source says 'stirring hot'.

A SOURCE REJECTED: a Pulse Ghana tuo zaafi page, byline the site's own name, printed date 5 February 2016 against a URL timestamp of 2024-08-03, with NO QUANTITIES. Its times are recorded for comparison only: corn flour mixture 5-10 minutes, 'Stir for 15-20 minutes before turning off heat'.
DRIED ROSEMARY in the marinade is not a traditional northern Ghanaian ingredient and is flagged rather than removed.
storage: The tuo is same-day. The stew keeps 4 days refrigerated; the ayoyo 2 days.
reheating: Steam the tuo. Reheat the stew gently; make the ayoyo fresh.
healthBenefits: Ayoyo (jute leaf) is very high in vitamins A, C and E, calcium and iron.
Dawadawa is a fermented food with documented B-vitamin content.
Beef or goat supplies protein, iron and vitamin B12.
The mucilage in ayoyo is a soluble fibre.
culturalNote: Tuo zaafi with ayoyo is the northern Ghanaian meal, and the slipperiness of the ayoyo is the whole point — it is what carries the tuo down. That the fullest written version of it is by a diaspora food writer rather than a northern Ghanaian cook is a real gap in the record, and it is stated rather than papered over.
